transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-05-13
- Time: 3:00 PM PT
- Duration: 48 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Liam (CTO Orbit), Priya (ML Eng), Samir (Product), Tara (Security)

Auto-generated summary (may be noisy):
Jordan opened with a quick context on Redwood's schema-first JSON mode for structured outputs and tool invocation. We demoed Console flow, API snippets, and Optimize recommendations for schemas, batching and guardrails. Orbit raised VPC/on-prem constraints, SOC2, latency vs cost tradeoffs; asked about typed outputs and automatic fallback to function calls. Next steps agreed: share sandbox notebook, security checklist, pricing, and schedule pilot kickoff.

Topics: JSON mode, schemas, function/tool calling, guardrails, Console demo, Optimize suggestions, VPC/private deployment, SOC2 & encryption, pilot scope and success metrics.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh really appreciate you carving out time. i'll do a 2 minute intro then hand over to maya who will run through a schema-first demo. mm-hmm
[00:14] Liam: yeah thanks, Jordan. quick note we've got schedule constraints — we need to lock a pilot in escalation by end of May if we want to include it in Q3 roadmap.
[00:23] Jordan: got it, that aligns. before maya starts, quick who-is who?
[00:28] Priya: priya here, ml engineer, mostly looking at how we'd integrate model outputs into our ETL and realtime scoring pipelines.
[00:35] Samir: samir, product manager, i'm here for UX and operational concerns — how predictable the output is.
[00:41] Tara: tara, security, i want to confirm data residency and encryption details.
[00:46] Jordan: perfect. maya over to you.
[00:48] Maya: cool thanks. i'll share my screen — show a brief Console flow then jump to an API example of JSON mode and a live function calling demo. note, screen's just a sample tenant not prod data.
[01:02] Maya: first slide: schema-first approach. the idea is you define a JSON schema (we support json-schema-ish shapes plus typed enums) and the runtime enforces output conformance, validation errors surfaced, and optional automatic tool invocation if structured output matches a tool signature. there are a couple of gotchas, like partial matches or noisy generation, we add guardrails and a typed fallback.
[01:30] Samir: when you say 'automatic tool invocation' do you call webhooks, or is it internal?
[01:35] Maya: good question — you can do both. most customers wire up function endpoints (http/webhook) or internal tools via our router. in the Console you map tool names to endpoints, set auth, and configure retries/fallbacks.
[01:48] Priya: and how strict is the schema? like if model returns null for a field, do you drop it or error?
[01:52] Maya: we have modes: strict (reject), best-effort (try to coerce), and enrich (call a helper tool to fill missing fields). for pilot you can run with best-effort then tighten to strict once prompt-sets pass.
[02:05] [Jordan chuckle] Jordan: something i always say: start lax then harden.
[02:12] Maya: live Console: i'm creating a 'transaction-enrichment' schema — fields: transaction_id (string), merchant (object with name and category enum), amount (number), risk_score (number 0-1), actions (array of tool-invocation objects). mapping tools: 'balance_lookup' -> internal account service, 'fraud_check' -> webhook to infra.
[02:35] Maya: ok i run a prompt against the sample model, JSON mode on, schema attached. watch the shaped output — notice the runtime validates and rewrites small types (like '100' -> 100) in best-effort.
[02:50] [Screen noise, keyboard clack]
[02:55] Maya: here's a case where model returns "merchant: 'ABC Grocery'" and we auto-enrich category with 'groceries' via a small tool call. the action object looks like {"tool": "fraud_check", "params": {"txn_id": "..."}} — that triggers a function call.
[03:10] Liam: so the function call happens synchronously? does it count as part of your token usage?
[03:15] Maya: function calls are orchestration-level; the model generates the call signature, Redwood routes it to the configured endpoint. tokens are charged for model generation; outbound request/response to your tool isn't token-billed but is part of runtime latency. we also trace it in Console for debugging.
[03:30] Tara: for security we need mTLS and KMS integration for secrets to call our internal endpoints. support?
[03:36] Maya: yes — we support mTLS to origin, integration with customer KMS/HSM for keys, and you can run this through Redwood Private in your VPC or on-prem package for air-gapped.
[03:50] Priya: regarding latency, if a prompt triggers multiple tool calls, does the model wait for results and then continue? how do you avoid tail latency?
[03:58] Ethan: typically you design calls that are low-latency or asynchronous. runtime supports streaming partial outputs and can emit a function call and continue with a stub response while backend completes; you can also configure timeouts and fallback to a default action. Optimize suggests batching and prewarming for common tool patterns to keep SLOs.
[04:20] Samir: can you show an API snippet? our infra team will use SDKs, not Console.
[04:25] Maya: sure. here's node example — we pass model: 'rwd-compat-3b', mode: 'json', schema: 'txn-enrich-v1', tools: [ {name: 'fraud_check', url: 'https://hooks.orbit.internal/fraud'} ] and callback_url for async.
[04:45] [Priya types: 'mm' sound]
[04:48] Priya: quick question — how do you handle hallucinated tool calls? e.g., model invents a tool name.
[04:53] Maya: good one — we restrict callable tools to the mapped set. any unmatched tool token is treated as output text unless you set strict tool whitelist which will throw and route to a policy fallback (like call a human review workflow).
[05:07] Jordan: and Optimize can run analysis across prompts to recommend tool whitelists and schema tightening to reduce those cases.
[05:15] Liam: what's Optimize exactly? is it a separate product?
[05:18] Maya: Optimize is our cost/perf toolkit — it analyzes usage patterns, suggests batching/quantization, cache policies, and schema changes to lower token cost while preserving quality. it also surfaces regressions tied to prompt/eval sets.
[05:32] Priya: our ops team wants to keep a single canonical schema in our repo. can we host schemas in S3 or Git and reference them?
[05:39] Maya: yep you can point the runtime at an S3/Git-hosted schema or upload to Console. during pilot we usually keep schemas in a shared repo and use the Console reference for quick iterations.
[05:49] [00:06 long pause; coffee sip noises]
[06:00] Maya: switching to a function-calling demo — i'll run a bad input to show guardrail behavior. prompt asks model to extract merchant and call fraud_check. model outputs a partial match, missing risk_score. we configured 'best-effort' so runtime fills risk_score via a small scoring tool; also we set a length limit and schema validation so oversized outputs get truncated and logged.
[06:30] Priya: curious about logs — are they PII redacted automatically? we have strict PII rules.
[06:36] Maya: yes, Console can redact configured fields and we integrate with customer DLP; in Private we give you full control. logs can be retained per your retention policy.
[06:45] Tara: SOC 2 question: do you publish SOC 2 reports?
[06:49] Jordan: yes we have SOC 2 Type II for hosted, and private deployments have an additional attestation path. we'll share the SOC 2 report and our compliance pack after the call.
[06:59] Liam: what's the overhead of strict schema enforcement on latency?
[07:03] Ethan: minimal on the model side — validation happens post-generation. the main overhead is if you use enrich mode and synchronous helper tools. Optimize can recommend moving enrichment offline or to async call patterns to keep 95th percentile latency tight.
[07:20] Samir: could you do a quick walk-through of a failure mode — e.g., if fraud_check fails, what happens?
[07:25] Maya: we have configurable fallbacks: retry policy, alternate endpoint, route to human-in-the-loop via a ticket, or mark the action as failed and continue with a default. Console shows the error trace and the raw model output.
[07:40] [08:00 timestamp hop while switching slides]
[08:05] Maya: live API test: i'm sending a batch of 12 small prompts, JSON mode with schema. you'll see batching stats in Console. Optimize flagged that for your workload a batch size of 8 with 2 worker threads hits a good throughput/latency sweet spot.
[08:25] [screen shows list of batch latencies: p50=120ms p95=430ms]
[08:30] Priya: those are good numbers. are these on rwd-compat-3b or larger?
[08:34] Maya: this is on a 7B quantized profile on dedicated GPUs. on hosted the numbers vary by region; we surface model profile in Console.
[08:42] Liam: about cost — what's our estimate for 1M calls per month with enrichment?
[08:46] Jordan: i'll send a model of three scenarios in the follow-up: hosted pay-as-you-go, Dedicated reserved with pilot commit, and Private license estimate. we'll include cost deltas for quantization and batching.
[08:58] Samir: do you support per-route SLOs and priority routing? we need to ensure critical routes get reserved capacity.
[09:05] Maya: yes — per-route SLOs, priority tiers, and you can pin a model version to a route. Redwood Dedicated supports reserved GPU pools for that.
[09:14] Tara: any customers doing encryption-in-use? like HSM-backed inference keys?
[09:19] Ethan: we support customer-managed keys and HSM for critical secrets; for inference in Private deployments you can also bring your own HSM.
[09:28] [09:30 short cross-talk 'yeah' 'okay']
[09:35] Priya: about developer experience — is there a local dev mode to test schemas without hitting production tokens?
[09:41] Maya: we provide a sandbox with local mocking of tools, sample models, and a dev SDK that emulates the runtime so you can iterate quickly. the notebook I'll share includes a harness for unit testing prompt/schema combos.
[09:55] Liam: what about observability — we need traces correlated to logs and token-level cost.
[10:01] Maya: Console has token-level cost per call, per-model, and tracing hooks that can correlate with your app traces. we also export to DataDog/Prometheus/ELK.
[10:12] Jordan: quick poll, does Orbit prefer hosted pilot or Dedicated isolated pool?
[10:18] Liam: security leans Dedicated or Private. if Dedicated can meet our compliance and latencies, that's ideal.
[10:25] Tar a: private is tricky for our procurement timeline; Dedicated with VPC peering and strict logging might be the quick path.
[10:33] Jordan: understood — we'll include both scenarios in the pricing.
[10:37] Maya: i'm going to show a tricky demo — schema with nested arrays and a function that expects a typed enum. watch how the runtime rejects incorrect enum values and suggests a soft-correction flag in Console.
[10:52] [console shows 'validation fail: merchant.category invalid -> suggested: "grocery"']
[10:57] Priya: that's neat. will you run an eval suite to measure fail rates?
[11:02] Maya: yes Optimize can run evals across sample prompts and track regressions. you can bind evals to PRs so schemas and prompts are gated.
[11:12] Samir: ok curious about development time — how long to ship a pilot integration?
[11:17] Jordan: our typical pilot is 2-4 weeks: week 0 onboarding & security review, week 1 schema & prompt setup, week 2 run pilot and optimize, week 3 iterate and measure. we can compress depending on Orbit's availability.
[11:30] Liam: are there case studies for fintech with similar compliance needs?
[11:33] Jordan: yes, we'll share a short case study and a benchmark spreadsheet.
[11:38] Maya: demo wrap-up — two short scenes: one where a function call succeeded and we enriched transaction, one where function call timed out and we routed to manual review. Console shows traces and the model output.
[11:55] [ambient typing]
[12:00] Tara: on the private deployment — what network features do you offer? we need IP allowlist, private endpoints, and audit logs.
[12:07] Ethan: we offer private control plane with customer-managed networking, VPC peering, IP allowlists, and full audit logs. those are available in Private or Dedicated with the right contract.
[12:18] Priya: did you mention KV cache earlier — can schema outputs reuse KV cache across sessions? we have repeated conversations per merchant.
[12:26] Maya: KV cache is per-model and can be keyed by prefix; you can cache recent merchant context to avoid repeated enrichment calls which saves cost. Optimize can recommend cache TTLs.
[12:36] Liam: what about fallback models if capacity spikes?
[12:40] Maya: smart routing can fallback to compatible model variants; we've got routing policies by latency or cost. live traffic continues with a lower-cost model if you permit it, and we log quality deltas.
[12:52] Samir: do you support function call chaining? e.g., model triggers A which triggers B and back to model?
[12:58] Maya: yes but you must configure allowed chains; we recommend limiting depth. you can also run asynchronous workflows in Redwood's orchestration that sequence calls outside the immediate model loop.
[13:12] [13:30 slight pause while screen switches to security doc]
[13:35] Jordan: tara, we'll attach our compliance pack. anything else we should include?
[13:40] Tara: include encryption at rest details, key rotation cadence, and incident response SLA.
[13:46] Jordan: noted.
[13:48] Maya: quick live note — i've instrumented an eval that shows tool-invocation hallucinations dropping after schema tightening by 78% in one case study.
[13:58] Priya: nice. can you add our prompt set to that eval?
[14:03] Maya: yes share the sample prompt list and we'll run it.
[14:08] Liam: procurement question — what does the Dedicated contract look like? is it monthly or annual?
[14:12] Jordan: Dedicated is typically annual reserved capacity with a month-to-month pilot addendum we can do for 60 days. the follow-up will include pricing options.
[14:22] Samir: any hard limits on calls or QPS?
[14:26] Ethan: we can set per-route quotas, burst capacity, and autoscaling policies. Dedicated gives you predictable throughput; hosted is more elastic but subject to tiers.
[14:38] [15:00 jump — demo nearing end]
[15:05] Maya: recap quick: - Schema-first JSON mode with strict/best-effort/enrich modes - Tools mapped and whitelisted; automatic invocation + function routing - Guardrails: validation, suggestion, fallback to human - Optimize suggestions for batching, caching, and model profiles - Private/Dedicated options for compliance
[15:30] Liam: good — from Orbit's side, next steps: we'll send a list of compliance docs, sample prompts and confirm pilot scope and size.
[15:37] Jordan: and from Redwood: we'll share sandbox notebook, SOC2 pack, pricing for hosted vs Dedicated, and schedule a pilot kickoff.
[15:45] Maya: action items logged in Console; i'll also email the notebook. links referenced: demo slides: https://redwood.example.com/shared/schema-tool-workshop.pdf sandbox notebook: https://redwood.example.com/sandbox/orbit-schema-demo.ipynb security pack: https://redwood.example.com/compliance/soc2.pdf
[15:58] Priya: thanks everyone, this was useful.
[16:02] Samir: thanks, curious to see the eval results.
[16:06] Tara: thanks — i'll follow up with security questions in email.
[16:10] Jordan: great thanks all — we'll follow up with next steps and pricing.
[16:15] [meeting ends]
